entries.paragraph_1: Pakistan Observer: Your business journey began in 1983 with Mian Tyre and Rubber Company. How did the company evolve into Panther Tyres, and what were the key milestones in its growth?
entries.paragraph_2: MIA: I started my business in 1983 under the name Mian Tyre and Rubber Company. As the business grew, people advised me in 2012 to bring the company’s name in line with its product brand, Panther Tyres. At that time, the product was already known as Panther Tyres, while the company was registered as Mian Tyre and Rubber Company. Following this advice, I changed the company’s name to align it with the brand. Initially, it was a private limited company. Later, we got it listed on the stock exchange, making it a publicly listed company. Our shares are now traded on the stock exchange, and we operate in accordance with the rules, regulations and procedures applicable to listed companies. By the grace of Allah, we have received a very encouraging response in the Pakistani market. Panther Tyres has become a popular brand, and I am proud of what we have achieved.

entries.title: AI chip smugglers exploit trade control loophole to bring banned HBM from South Korea into China — expensive memory chips packaged with cheap, unsanctioned processors to become legal exports | Tom's Hardware
entries.paragraph_1: A memory smuggler has detailed how he gets export-controlled HBM chips from South Korea into China using a loophole. According to The Information , the smuggler owns a chip design firm that build cheap, low-performing processors that fall under the U.S. and South Korea’s export controls. They are then paired with expensive HBM from Samsung and SK hynix, that, on their own, are banned for export to China. But because export control rules only look at the performance of the server processor and not at the other components attached to it, this allows the HBM chips attached inside them to slip under the radar and make their way into China.
entries.paragraph_2: It’s not a risk-free operation, though. Once the mediocre processors with high-end memory chips land in Hong Kong and are smuggled across the border into Shenzhen in the luggage of commuters that cross between the two regions daily, they end up in workshops where technicians heat up the boards to soften the solder, gingerly lift the crucial memory chips, and discard the rest of the components. Despite having a high failure rate, the high price of HBM chips makes the procedure quite lucrative.

entries.title: Electric auto rickshaws reshape India's roads | The Peninsula Qatar
entries.paragraph_1: Photograph taken on October 22, 2026, shows a customer driving his newly purchased Mahindra UDO electric three wheeler in India's Telangana state. (Photo by Noah Seelam / AFP)
entries.paragraph_2: Hyderabad, India: Every 90 seconds, an electric three-wheeler rolls off the production line at an Indian factory, underscoring a transformation that has made the country the largest market for battery-powered auto rickshaws. At a bustling plant run by Mahindra Last Mile Mobility, workers and robots fit cells into battery packs, attach body panels to metal frames and fix wheels into place, racing to meet demand for vehicles known for navigating the chaotic streets of the world's most populous country. In September, more than one in two new three-wheelers sold in India was electric, compared with about 8.5 percent of cars and 11.6 percent of two-wheelers, reaffirming its position as the world's largest electric three-wheeler market. "Our company has grown six times in its EV penetration in the last five years," said Mahindra LMM's chief executive Suman Mishra. She said adoption accelerated over the past two years as government subsidies, improving vehicle quality and falling operating costs combined to make ownership more attractive. E-rickshaws first appeared on New Delhi's streets more than a decade ago, often assembled in roadside workshops using Chinese-made batteries fitted to modified pedal-powered tricycles. But the sector has since eaten into the market for sturdier fossil-fuel-powered three-wheelers, becoming a major industry as manufacturers such as Mahindra expand their share. The shift has altered the look and sound of Indian cities. Across northern India, e-rickshaws now queue outside railway stations and bustling markets, replacing the thumping noise of traditional "tuk-tuks". Fuel savings Mahindra is one of 15 finalists shortlisted for the environmental Earthshot Prize, to be awarded in Mumbai by Prince William on November 17. For many drivers, however, earnings outweigh environmental benefits. "Money is coming straight into my pocket," said Afroz Alam, a 31-year-old driver in Hyderabad who switched from a gas-powered model to an EV this year. The cost of charging his vehicle saves him several hundred rupees a day, helping repay the loan he took out to buy the more expensive electric version. "It may seem expensive, but then it levels out with the gas money you no longer have to pay," he told AFP. Analysts agree economics is the key driver of adoption, with falling costs of batteries and rising fuel prices widening the advantage of e-vehicles. Indian think-tank CEEW estimated in 2025 that petrol three-wheelers cost more than twice as much per kilometre to operate over their lifetime as EVs. "Rickshaws, which operate continuously throughout the day, accumulate fuel savings rapidly," said Bidisha Bhattacharya of the Delhi-based Chintan Research Foundation. The trend has also been welcomed by policymakers in India, which imports most of its oil and natural gas and has scrambled to manage energy costs, since conflict in the Middle East erupted in February. Climate think-tank Ember said India consumes less transport fuel per capita than China did at a comparable income level in 2012, helped by the spread of cheap solar power and declining battery costs. "In the race to curb oil imports, India is already far ahead," Ember said in a recent report. Yet hurdles remain, with adoption uneven across the country. 'Battery will fail' E-rickshaws are common in cities such as Lucknow but far less visible in Mumbai, where limited parking and charging infrastructure complicate ownership. "In Mumbai, there is no parking at all," Mishra said. "So you can park on the side of the road for a (fuel-run) vehicle, but how do you do it for an EV when you have to charge it?" Supply chains pose another challenge. Last year, China restricted exports of rare-earth magnets, an essential component in electric motors, forcing several Indian automakers to cut or suspend production. New Delhi has responded by promoting domestic manufacturing, including battery cells, most of which are still imported from China and South Korea. "Two players are very close to commercialisation of their cells in India. We have to be patient," Mishra said. The bigger question is whether the success of e-rickshaws can be replicated in private cars and, eventually, trucks, which consume far more fuel. Bhattacharya said commercial fleets could provide the next breakthrough. When taxis transition to electric power, she said, they would help build the charging networks and consumer confidence. For drivers already making the switch, the argument remains simple. "They keep saying the battery will fail," said Mohammad Ali, 26, who bought an e-rickshaw this year. "Do a trial, take the vehicle and do it for a day. They don't know yet how much money we are saving."

entries.title: [Editorial] US contradicting itself by pressuring S. Korea to extend GSOMIA
entries.paragraph_1: As we approach the termination of South Korea and Japan’s GSOMIA military intelligence-sharing agreement, scheduled for Nov. 23, the US is exerting intense pressure on South Korea to reverse its decision to terminate the agreement. But the decision to terminate was a reluctant countermeasure taken by the South Korean government against Japan’s economic retribution. The US is contradicting itself when it claims it has no intention of intervening in the South Korea-Japan conflict only to take issue with South Korea’s GSOMIA termination. If the US is truly concerned about the agreement being scrapped, the first thing it ought to do is push Japan to retract the economic retribution that drove South Korea to make that decision in the first place.

entries.title: [Column] The South Korea-US security meeting can wait
entries.paragraph_1: By Jung E-gil, senior international affairs writer
entries.paragraph_2: The US midterm elections on Tuesday mark a major turning point for Seoul’s relations with Washington and its foreign policy more broadly. The outcome will have a profound impact on the domestic and foreign policies of US President Donald Trump, who has plunged both his own country and the international community into turmoil. Even if the Democrats win, Trump could refuse to accept the results or simply ignore them and double down on his policies. His threat to resume attacks on Iran after the midterms is a case in point. Nevertheless, an election defeat would undermine Trump’s authority and his ability to carry out his agenda. Trump’s signature initiatives — including his war against Iran, his efforts to end the war in Ukraine, and his trade and tariff campaign against countries around the world — have ground to a halt over the past few months. Facing resistance from the countries affected, Trump has put off further negotiations until after the midterms. Despite Trump’s threats to resume attacks, Iran has steadfastly refused to negotiate unless the seven conditions in its seven-day confidence-building plan are met. Those conditions include the US lifting its naval blockade and releasing frozen assets. Separately, Russia has agreed to participate in US-mediated three-party talks with Ukraine but postponed them until after the midterms. Moscow has secured partial relief from US sanctions, including restrictions on diesel exports, while refusing to budge on its current conditions for ending the fighting. Canada, which has been one of the fiercest opponents of Trump’s trade onslaught, also persuaded him to withdraw the 50% tariffs he had imposed before postponing a new trade agreement until the midterms are over. While discussing the two countries’ trade talks on Oct. 26, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said that “to the extent any progress has been made, it’s because the US is coming closer to our position.”

entries.paragraph_1: North Korea fired several missiles toward the sea off its east coast on Wednesday, hours after Kim Yo Jong, the sister of leader Kim Jong Un, said Pyongyang saw no need for talks with Washington, and two weeks before President Donald Trump travels to Asia for a regional summit where a meeting with Kim had been floated. South Korea's Joint Chiefs of Staff said the missiles were launched from the Sondok area in South Hamgyong province and flew less than 300 kilometers before falling into the sea. It was the fourth weapons launch by North Korea in a month.
entries.paragraph_2: The Joint Chiefs said South Korea and the United States monitored preparations for the launch and tracked the missiles immediately after liftoff, and that they were analyzing the missiles' specifications, including whether more than one type was fired. The U.S. Indo-Pacific Command said, according to a report of its statement, that the launches did not pose an immediate threat to American personnel, territory or allies. Japan's coast guard asked ships to stay alert.

entries.paragraph_1: The development came ahead of the 33rd Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Summit, scheduled on Nov. 18 and 19 in China. The meeting placed the North Korean nuclear file on the agenda of a gathering otherwise focused on global economic policy. They also highly evaluated the activities of the Multinational Sanctions Monitoring Team, the body tasked with tracking sanctions enforcement [1] . The State Departmentâs readout did not indicate that the ministers announced new measures, set a timetable for renewed negotiations or disclosed any direct contact with North Korean officials. North Korea Maintains Nuclear-Armed Status North Korea continues to reject disarmament and has enshrined its status as a nuclear-armed state in law. Pyongyang has ruled out giving up its weapons, a stance that has outlasted successive rounds of diplomacy and pressure campaigns. The Northâs position rests on a security calculation that outside analysts have long described: the regime views its arsenal as the ultimate guarantee against external pressure, and it has shown little willingness to trade that guarantee for economic relief alone [2] . Academic assessments of nuclear proliferation have noted that the most consequential step in the process is the acquisition of fissile material, and that once a state crosses that threshold, reversing course becomes substantially harder [2] . The North is backed by Russia and China, whose diplomatic cover has blunted international enforcement. Moscow and Beijing have worked to soften successive rounds of sanctions, according to published analyses of the Security Council process [3] . That support has given Pyongyang room to weather restrictions that would otherwise have imposed higher costs. North Korea also denounced a Saturday joint statement by a group of nations monitoring sanctions implementation. Trump Overtures and APEC Summit Speculation Speculation is mounting over a possible meeting between the U.S. and North Korea. No meeting has been confirmed, and neither government has announced preparations for one. The report stated that U.S President Donald Trump conceded last year that North Korea was already âsort of a nuclear powerâ and said he was â100%â open to a meeting. That suggestion went unanswered. The absence of a reply has left the diplomatic track stalled. The reported visit, if confirmed, would suggest the North is coordinating its approach with its principal ally rather than responding directly to Washington. The APEC summit would provide a venue for a leaders-level encounter without the formal preparation that a dedicated bilateral summit would require. Regional Positions and Debate Over a Freeze South Korean President Lee Jae Myung, who has offered talks without preconditions, suggested in September that Washington seek a freeze rather than the immediate elimination of the Northâs nuclear program in return for sanctions relief. The proposal marked a shift in emphasis from the position the three allies restated in Atlanta. Critics have said such an approach risks tacitly accepting North Korea as a nuclear-armed state and allowing Pyongyang to obtain sanctions relief without giving up its arsenal. The debate turns on whether a freeze would lock in the Northâs capabilities or serve as a first step toward broader limits. Analysts say China may also be moving toward tacit acceptance. They point to the omission of North Korean denuclearization from statements issued after North Korean leader Kim Jong-Un and Chinese President Xi Jinping met in June. The omission, analysts argue, could signal that Beijing is prepared to treat the Northâs arsenal as a settled fact rather than a negotiating objective. The competing positions leave the three allies with a stated goal of complete denuclearization and an array of tactical options that range from pressure to conditional engagement. entries.title: Enshrined Conflict: The Paradox of the Yasukuni Shrine - Brown Political Review
entries.paragraph_1: The 1946 Tokyo War Crimes Trials , carried out by the Allied powers during postwar occupation, marked one of the first attempts to reckon with the atrocities committed by the Japanese Army during the Second World War. 28 men, many of whom were architects of the war, were indicted on charges of “Class A” war crimes for directing aggression that led to crimes against humanity. The trials represented an initial but important effort to reconcile a violence-filled past waged across East Asia. However, the legacy of the trials became far more complicated 30 years later, when 14 Class A criminals were enshrined in the Yasukuni shrine—a monument in the heart of Tokyo meant to honor those who gave their lives in service to the Japanese military. Since then, the shrine has been the subject of heated debate and constant controversy. After all, the 14 men were responsible for millions of deaths. The shrine also honors 2.5 million others who gave their lives in service of Japan throughout history, many of whom never saw the battlefield. As such, visits have been justified as an important remembrance for all of those who gave their life for the nation, a remembrance that should not be diluted by the inclusion of a small percentage of war criminals. At first glance, the shrine seems to propose a straightforward moral tension: how should a nation honor sacrifice while acknowledging horrific wrongdoing in its past? But this framing is incomplete. Controversy around Yasukuni persists because it attempts to serve two legitimate but ultimately opposing purposes. As a Shinto landmark, it seeks to nonjudgementally honor the dead and provide the living with a means to fulfill religious obligations; as a political symbol, it appears to affirm a hypernationalist, negationist, and revisionist view of history that at best denies and at worst glorifies past atrocities. As long as the shrine is asked to serve this dual function, any conflict surrounding it will remain irresolvable.
entries.paragraph_2: Yasukuni—which translates to “to preserve peace for the entire nation”—is a Shinto shrine, placing it within a religious framework that does not and cannot make moral distinctions between the dead. Shinto is Japan’s indigenous religion , centered around the worship of divine spirits. The shrine was established in 1869 by Emperor Meiji in the wake of a civil war to honor those who died and gave their souls for the Emperor. In Shinto belief, the dead become Kami , a rough equivalent to the word “spirit” or “deity.” Crucially, Shinto followers see death as inherently tragic no matter what, and believe there is no evaluative judgment of the dead or delineation into heaven or hell. On the contrary, it is up to the living, through rituals and worship, to ensure a peaceful transition and a fruitful afterlife for all of the dead and to maintain harmony between the living and spiritual realms. Within this logic, the enshrinement of war criminals in Yasukuni is not necessarily a statement on morality, history, or national memory; it is simply the fulfillment of a religious obligation to the communal war dead, regardless of the actions of specific individuals within that group.

entries.title: Экс-глава LG в России Енгнам Ро захотел стать мостом между РФ и Южной Кореей - Новости Mail
entries.paragraph_1: Бывший руководитель LG Electronics в России и странах СНГ , а по совместительству южнокорейский поэт Енгнам Ро заявил, что хотел бы стать «мостом» между Россией и Южной Кореей. Об этом он сказал на встрече с российскими журналистами в Сеуле.
entries.paragraph_2: По словам Ро, накопленный за годы работы в бизнесе опыт и связи между странами могут помочь ему в этой миссии. Он понимает, что литература и искусство не решат международные конфликты мгновенно, но верен тому, что даже в периоды политических разногласий они оставляют пространство для взаимопонимания.
